Reference Benchmark, TutorBench: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02663](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02663)  
Tutor Bench Notes:  
Sample from dataset: ![][image1]  
Uses actual images of students work for better personalization capability testing. Rubric based evaluation with LLM judge, rubrics are human made(experts) same as questions, both are verifiable. Specifically makes benchmark challenging by only choosing samples that at least 3 of 5 LLMs scored \<50% on.  
**Three use cases:**  
Adaptive Explanaiton Geneation:

- Identify core misconceptions and shortcomings in students understanding and adapt explanatinos to them  
- Initial question in student persona, initial explanation from tutor persona, follow up question in student persona, model needs to generate an explanation to respond to follow up   
- Found that models score only 47.16 on adaptive explanation on average

Assessment and feedback:

- Abiiltiy to assess work, classify mistakes and give feedback  
- Models are shown student solutions and have to assess it  
- Typically averaged 51.56 for most models, 

Active Learning Support:

- Ability to ensure students are engaged with problem solving, this means scaffolding with hints and analogies so students still have agency.   
- Models have to generastre helpful hints for the next step without giving away answer  
- Claude models perforemd much better at this

Judging: 

- Single model, 3 to 39 criteria rubric weighted from non-critical and critical 1 or 5 with \-5 for undesirable behaviors  
- Normalized final score to 0,1  
- Quality verification with 3 human ratings per criterion on 250 sample subset, judge aligns better with human experts than median human, F1 score of .81

Multidimensional tagging for each rubric criteria, with general model tags and tutoring skill tags. Also explicit/implicit tags, with explicit meaning the prompt asked for it and objective/subjective tags, for factual vs subjective standards(tone…)

Issues:

- 3 of 5 \<50 % removal can cause bias and lower all scores naturally.   
- Single model llm judge, potential bias  
- Scoring isnt pyschometrically standardized  
- No IRT for proper latent ability validation and discrimination/difficulty standardization  
- No CAT, 1490 samples for LLMs to go through  
- Doesnt include practice problem generation, concept introduction  
- Only evaluates one response  
- No humanities evaluation  
- Many samples are multimodal, requiring extra

[https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11106](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11106)  Fluid  
Claims:  
(1) it can produce better eval results while using up to 50 times fewer questions  
(2) it reduces score changes caused by measurement noise so progress across training checkpoints are easier to track  
(3) it continues to measure improvement after accuracy scores begin to flatten near the top of a benchmark

**Experimental Setup**

- Model evaluation during pretraining  
- 6 Open LLM benchmarks    
- IRT models calibrated using responses of 102 pretrained language models  
- Tested on 6 held out models 2.8 B \- 65 B parameters

**IRT Calibration**

- Separate 2 parameter IRT model is fitted for each benchmark  
  - Model estimates difficulty (ability a model needs to answer correctly) \+ discrimination (how well an item separates models with different ability levels) of each benchmark item  
- IRT models fitted using the complete response patterns of the 102 calibration models \-\> item parameters fixed, used to estimate ability of new models

**How it works**

- Starts with an estimate of the model’s current ability  
- Selects unused item that provides the most information about a model at that ability level  
- After response, FLUID updates model’s ability estimate \-\> used to choose next most informative item  
- Evaluation stops after fixed length (10, 50, 100, 500\)  
- Final score \= model’s estimated IRT ability

**Implications/Limitations**

- Lower measurement noise \-\> small changes between checkpoints easier to separate from random score changes  
- Paper tests general language model benchmarks rather than pedagogical skills  
- Most held out models \~7B parameters  
- Each benchmark represented by one overall ability  
- Requires response data from many diverse models to calibrate items

[https://arxiv.org/html/2511.04689v2](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.04689v2)  ATLAS

Claims:  
(1) it reduces computational cost by requiring 90% fewer items while maintaining overall performance  
(2) it overcomes the ceiling effects of accuracy-based metrics and preserves discrimination across the ability spectrum  
(3) it distinguishes models with identical accuracy score but different abilities \<- very important for pedagogy benchmarking  
(4) it outperforms TinyBenchmarks (mentioned by name), only requiring 30–89 items per benchmark to score reliably and having a lower Information Efficiency Score (IES) 

**Steps:**

**Data Construction**

* Collect Data from Benchmarks  
* Filtering  
  * remove unsuitable models (below the 0.1st percentile in ability)  
  * eliminate non-informative items  
    * Items with response standard deviation \< 1% or \>95% mean accuracy are removed  
    * Items that have less than .1 correlation with models performance on the whole benchmark are removed (point-biserial correlation) 	  
* Get models and stratify by token size  
  * Although since we only care about 1bn param models, we will probably only get a sample of those  
* Train/Test split with models  
  * 90% models used to calibrate IRT  
  * 10% models used to take CAT and see if score matches benchmark score

**IRT Calibration**  
Idea is rather than calibrating on the whole item Set, split it up calibrate, then recombine because each set is being calibrated by the same set of models so they can be merged with that as reference

* Divide into K non-overlapping subsets   
* All models used for all subsets (act as common persons)  
* Model Fit Validation (i don’t really understand this, but they do something called the M2 test)  
* Then just use normal 3PL model to calibrate each subset  
* Align and merge subsets (Also don’t full understand how this happens)

**IRT Model**

- Uses a two-parameter multidimensional IRT model, which varies difficulty (b) and discrimination (a). a and b are estimated for each item in the benchmark set.  
- Performance-IRT estimator: we are interested in estimating essentially the average “correctness,” which translates to correctness rate.  
- We estimate LLM ability level based on responses from a subset of examples. To do so, we take the theta value that maximizes the log likelihood of obtaining that specific set of responses.  
1. Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) based on difficulty, distribution, etc  
- Mathematically, the process becomes equivalent to fitting a logistic regression model (theta is the parameter being fit).  
- Especially useful if we fit data through many scenarios: multiple subsets from the same set of examples.   
- Generalize P-IRT estimator: iteration on P-IRT, assigns p-irt trust level based on predicted bias.

[https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.19275](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.19275) 

3PL \- IRT model used by ATLAS is typically unidimensional, we could do a multidimensional

Basic difference between unidimensional and multidimensional is:  
Within a single question:  
Each answer choice is more or less wrong

Between questions:  
Limit the exact skills that a question targets, taking the venn diagram of different questions to isolate specific skills ability level

In CAT lingo this is called (latent traits).

[https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.00521](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.00521) \- graded response model

Idea: can’t tell if LLM judge is a good/stable measurement tool by just raw scores, so use IRT 

- Reliability \= task, rubric, prompt, rating scale

Method: 

- Graded response model:  
  - ![][image4]  
  - Theta represents latent ability associated with response J  
  - Alpha is discrimination of prompt p, how steeply the ratings vary with small quality differences  
  - Beta is threshold when prompt gives a rating of k or higher, point where response has a 50% chance of \>= k score  
- Tests judges by introducing minor changes like typos, newlines, and paraphrases, if they respond severely then not as reliable  
  - Measured with Cv, prompt consistency, aims to have consistent responses despite prompt variations  
  - Also tests Marginal reliability to see how much variances reflect true quality diffs  
- Tests similarity between LLM’s judges quality perception and human judgments  
  - Also scales LLM rating range vs Human rating range

Findings:

- Small changes to the grading prompt changed how some LLM judges assigned score categories  
- GRM helped separate real differences in response quality, accounts for judge bias/sensitivity   
- None of the LLM judges were reliable for every eval criteria

If we implement LLM judge I think this model would help us standardize for discrimination.

**Pedagogy Benchmark:**  
[https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.18710](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.18710)  
Pulls questions from chilean teachers exam, cleaned extracted translated and deduped to 1143 questions.   
Used 4o mini for ocr and translation, with a small amount cross-checked by human.  
Some questions were also removed because they were incorrect on 31/36 models,  
Special education category(SEND) was separated to a separate benchmark, 223 questions, 920 remained.   
All of them were inspected by a pedagogy expert who edited the questions, 21 questions were designated as few-shot, 899 weren’t few-shot.   
Standard deviation across 20 runs for 8 models was .43% maximum, showing stability between runs.   
95% bootstrap intervals from 1000 item-level resamples.   
Did acknowldge model token/positional bias in mcqs, showing that through targeted tests, models sometimes preferred A and sometimes didn’t prefer D.   
Human teachers average on this is expected to be 50% but estimated since their per-question answers arent revealed and they don’t test on every subject, just their own.  
SEND and main scores correlate at 0.94, both tests measure common general capability  

Stated limitations:

- Some differences between leading models were low  
- Single question source  
- Chilean bias and translation issues, 

Other limitations 

- Item answers arent standardized with any form of IRT  
- No skills check with multidimensional either  
- Long benchmark, optimization potential  
- Only MCQs, shown to have bias   
- Potentially removied valid but hard questions during cleaning when 10% were removed due to low performance across the board.  
- Not compared with MMLU or other popular benchmarks for correlation.   
- Only measures knowledge about pedagogy.
